newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Veteran Maori campaigner and NZ lawmaker Rata dies.
newsitem.headline: Veteran Maori campaigner and NZ lawmaker Rata dies.

text.p: Maori campaigner and former New Zealand minister Matiu Rata died on Friday aged 63, national news media reported.
Rata, 63, had suffered multiple injuries in a car crash in northern North Island last weekend and died at Auckland Hospital of kidney failure, the New Zealand Press Association said.

In a career largely devoted to campaigning for Maori rights and causes, Rata earned his place in history by paving the way for the creation of a tribunal to consider breaches of the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi between Maori and European settlers.
He guided the forming act through parliament in 1975 and then continued to press for extension of the Waitangi Tribunal's mandate for another 10 years.
Former Labour prime minister Sir Geoffrey Palmer called Rata the catalyst behind the modern Maori renaissance.
"The setting up of the Waitangi Tribunal, which was his work, has been an enduring contribution to the constitutional position of Maoris in this country," he said.
Named minister of Maori affairs and minister of lands by an incoming Labour government in 1970, Rata served under two prime ministers until the party was ousted in 1975.
He spent five more years in parliament before breaking from Labour in 1979 after being dropped from its front bench team.
After serving briefly as an independent he formed the Maori party, Mana Motuhake, and quit the house to test the mood of his electorate at a by-election in June 1980.
Although he failed to be re-elected he pressed on with the cause and the party has since become represented after last year's first elections under a proportional voting system.
Current Mana Motuhake leader Sandra Lee described Rata as a visionary.
"We should all consider as New Zealanders what the landscape would be like if we did not have the legislation he brought in," she said.
